summary:
Khanty-Mansiysk Autonomous Okrug – Ugra stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which applies in full. No regional deviation from that regime was identified in the sources, so the national findings below govern what a transgender visitor faces in the okrug.

Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage is prohibited and legal gender transition has been banned outright since 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and gender changes on official documents took effect. Document gender markers can no longer be altered, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in the same year.

The expanded propaganda statute criminalises public expression of LGBT themes, including anything that, in its wording, "justifies" gender transition. First offences are punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days; a repeat offence carries up to four years' imprisonment. Since the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation in 2023, participation in that movement carries two to six years and organising it six to ten years.

Foreigners are exposed directly. The US State Department advisory for Russia states that nationals of other countries found guilty of violating the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and then deported, that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime, and it advises against all travel to Russia.

Enforcement has produced a measurable toll. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions, about 98 administrative and three criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted across 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024. It assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution and that the state is able but unwilling to protect them, and it affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Official warnings to travellers reflect these findings: national government advisories tell LGBT visitors plainly that arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation are the consequences of violating these statutes.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement climate has intensified as well as broadened. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget over the two preceding years.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where roughly 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Pretrial detention carries lethal risk in these cases. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Coercive practices against transgender people are documented alongside the statutory regime. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

Official hostility is not confined to statute. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life through 2025 according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as a second-class citizen after the designation. The autonomous republic of Chechnya appears in the UK Home Office note as an extreme instance of the same national condition rather than a separate legal order.
localsOnly:
Residents of the okrug live under the same prohibitions as visitors, with the additional exposure of having no route out of them through documents: gender markers on Russian official documents cannot be changed, so a resident's legal gender is fixed at birth regardless of social or medical transition.

Medical transition is unavailable lawfully. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, closing the clinical pathway that residents had previously used, and gender reassignment surgery is prohibited by statute.

Marriage and family recognition are closed to same-sex couples: same-sex marriage is banned, and no partnership recognition regime exists at national level.

Ordinary expression exposes residents to penalty without any foreign-traveller dimension. Displaying banned symbols under article 20.3 produced 98 administrative cases and 81 convictions between January 2024 and June 2025, while article 282.2 charges carry up to 12 years; the Home Office counted at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.

The Home Office assessment is that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution and that the state is able but unwilling to protect them. For residents, that finding describes the protection machinery itself: the domestic authorities do not stand between the affected population and organised hostility, and the designated extremist label supplies legal cover for it.

Residents who leave the country are assessed by the UK asylum system as members of a particular social group under the refugee convention, the standard against which UK claims are measured.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports enforcement specific to Khanty-Mansiysk Autonomous Okrug – Ugra: no arrests, raids, administrative cases or court proceedings from the okrug are documented, and the regional picture is carried entirely by national-level data.

The okrug's own authorities have issued no located statement, instruction or protective measure on gender identity or sexual orientation, so whether regional police or prosecutors apply the national statutes at a higher or lower rate than elsewhere is unresolved.

No source addresses practical access to documentation, border-crossing screening, or the treatment of a foreign passport bearing a gender marker inconsistent with presentation at airports or checkpoints serving the okrug; that risk is inferred from the national advisory rather than observed.

No data was located on local support organisations, safe accommodation, or healthcare access of any kind for transgender residents within the okrug, and none can be confirmed from the sources used here.

The Home Office note's count of 139 impacted people covers 2022 to 2024 and is not broken down by region, so the share attributable to the okrug remains unknown.
